hints: Start by naming the functional group in each of J, K, L and M from Fig. 4.1, then match each reagent to the functional groups it is known to test for.
Recall which types of compound reduce orange acidified dichromate to green Cr(III), thinking about aldehydes versus ketones and primary versus secondary alcohols.
Recall the structural requirement for the iodoform reaction with alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$, the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group in carbonyls and the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$ group in alcohols.
Recall which reagent gives an orange precipitate only with aldehydes and ketones, and why J and K share this result.
Recall what type of hydrogen reacts with $\text{Na(s)}$ to give effervescence of $\text{H}_2$, and decide which two of J to M contain $\text{O-H}$ bonds.
walkthrough:
Label J to M so you know what can react**
Look closely at Fig. 4.1. J is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, an aldehyde. K is $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, a ketone and also a methyl ketone. L is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, a secondary alcohol containing a $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$ group. M is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, a carboxylic acid. Once you have these labels, each test becomes a simple functional group match.

Acidified dichromate, the oxidation test**
Acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7\text{(aq)}$ is an oxidising agent. It oxidises aldehydes to carboxylic acids, and primary and secondary alcohols to carbonyls or acids, while itself is reduced from orange $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ to green $\text{Cr}^{3+}$. So J (aldehyde) and L (secondary alcohol) are oxidised and give orange to green. K (ketone) and M (already a carboxylic acid) show no change.

Alkaline iodine, the iodoform test**
Alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$ gives a yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$ only with methyl ketones containing $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ and methyl secondary alcohols containing $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$. That is exactly K and L. J is an aldehyde without a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group, and M is a carboxylic acid, so both are negative.

Orange precipitate, the carbonyl test**
An orange precipitate is the classic positive result with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, often called 2,4-DNPH or Brady's reagent. It reacts by condensation with the $\text{C=O}$ of aldehydes and ketones. That fits J and K perfectly, while the alcohol L and the acid M do not give this test.

Sodium metal, the acidic hydrogen test**
$\text{Na(s)}$ reacts with any compound containing an $\text{O-H}$ group that can release $\text{H}_2$ gas, seen as effervescence: $2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_2$. Both L (alcohol $\text{O-H}$) and M (carboxylic acid $\text{O-H}$) have this, while J and K have no $\text{O-H}$ bond. So the observation is effervescence and the compounds are L and M.

Final answer: Row 1: observation (solution turns from) orange to green.
Row 2: compounds K and L.
Row 3: reagent 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine / 2,4-DNPH.
Row 4: observation effervescence; compounds L and M.

hints: Identify the electrophilic centre in K by considering the polarity of the $\text{C=O}$ bond and where the $\delta+$ charge sits.
Recall how a nucleophile such as $:\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks, thinking about where the curly arrow starts (lone pair) and where it points.
Think about what happens to the $\text{C=O}$ pi electrons when the new $\text{C-C}$ bond forms, and what intermediate this creates on oxygen.
Consider how the negatively charged oxygen intermediate is converted into the final $\text{OH}$ group in N.
walkthrough:
Spot why the carbonyl carbon is attacked**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the $\text{C=O}$ in $\text{H}_3\text{C-CO-C}_2\text{H}_5$ is polarised as $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$. Mark these dipoles clearly. The $\delta+$ carbon is electron poor, so it is the electrophile that attracts the nucleophile.

Attack by cyanide and breaking of the pi bond**
The nucleophile is $:\text{CN}^{-}$, with its lone pair on carbon. Draw a curly arrow starting at that lone pair and pointing to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$. At the same time, draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond up onto the oxygen. This shows the pi electrons moving onto oxygen as the new $\text{C-CN}$ bond forms.

Draw the alkoxide intermediate correctly**
After attack you get a tetrahedral intermediate: central C bonded to $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$, $\text{CN}$ and $\text{O}^{-}$. Show the full negative charge and a lone pair on oxygen. This $\text{O}^{-}$ is strongly basic and will pick up a proton.

Protonation to give the hydroxynitrile N**
Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{HCN}$. This forms the $\text{O-H}$ bond of N, $\text{H}_3\text{C-C(OH)(CN)-C}_2\text{H}_5$, and regenerates $:\text{CN}^{-}$, which is why $\text{KCN}$ is a catalyst.

Final answer: Show $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ on $\text{C=O}$ of K.
Curly arrow from lone pair on $:\text{CN}^{-}$ to $\text{C}^{\delta+}$; curly arrow from $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{O}$ to give $(\text{CH}_3)(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)\text{C(O}^{-})(\text{CN})$ intermediate.
Curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to $\text{H}^{+}$ (from $\text{HCN}$) to give N.

hints: Look at the two functional groups now attached to the same carbon in N, an $\text{OH}$ group and a $\text{CN}$ group, and recall the combined name for this class.
walkthrough:
Name the class from both groups together**
N contains $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CN}$ on the same carbon, $\text{H}_3\text{C-C(OH)(CN)-C}_2\text{H}_5$. A compound with a hydroxy group and a nitrile group in this arrangement belongs to the hydroxynitrile class, also called a cyanohydrin.

hints: Focus on the central carbon in N and count how many different groups are bonded to it to explain why it is chiral.
walkthrough:
Explain chirality as four different attachments**
A chiral centre is a carbon with four different atoms or groups attached to it. In N the central C is bonded to $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CN}$, all different, so it has no plane of symmetry and can exist as non-superimposable mirror images.
Final answer: A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms / (functional) groups.
